Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

depictr (development version)

Figures that misreported the data

  • estimation_plot(), and group_comparison_plot(differences = TRUE) which calls it, failed in a fresh R session with “Can’t find method for generic /(e1, e2)”, or with “non-numeric argument to binary operator” under ggplot2 3.5. The two panels were stacked with patchwork’s / operator, which exists only once patchwork has been loaded, and nothing in depictr loaded it. The panels are now composed with patchwork::wrap_plots(), and depictr imports patchwork, so library(depictr) loads it.

  • estimation_plot() drew the differences out of line with the groups they belong to. The lower panel had one column fewer than the upper and spread its columns across the full width, so with reference North, the East difference sat beneath North, and with two groups, the single difference sat midway between them. Every group now keeps its column in both panels, and the reference’s column in the lower panel is left empty. group_comparison_plot(differences = TRUE) is fixed with it. The function is also described for what it draws, a Cumming estimation plot with the differences stacked beneath the data. The claim that zero lines up with the reference group’s mean has been removed, since the stacked panels have independent axes. The caption now writes a round number of resamples in full, as 100,000 where it printed 1e+05.

  • coefficient_plot() attached an unnamed labels vector to the wrong coefficients. The labels were assigned after the terms had been reversed or sorted for display, so in lm(yield ~ rainfall + fertiliser + soil_ph) soil pH was labelled ‘Rainfall’. An unnamed vector is now bound to the terms in model order before any reordering. compare_models() and frequentist_bayesian_plot() counted one row per term and source, or one per posterior draw, and so refused a vector with one label per term. Both now accept one, read with the terms in the order they first appear. Named labels are unchanged and remain the safer form. The documentation of order now says which end the largest estimate lands at.

  • model_fit_table() and the model_report() subtitle misreported R² for glm models. McFadden’s ratio was applied to every family, so a Gaussian glm could report a negative value and a quasi-likelihood family reported NA. The null model was refitted with update(). That used more rows than the model when a predictor had missing values, dropped an offset written in the formula, put an intercept in the null of a model fitted without one and gave NA for a model fitted inside a function. Every glm, including quasi-likelihood and negative binomial fits, now reports the deviance R², 1 - D/D0, computed from the deviances the fit already holds. It equals the ordinary R² for a Gaussian model with the identity link and McFadden’s R² for binary logistic regression, so a binary logistic value changes only where the old refit went wrong. Values for Poisson, grouped binomial, Gamma and other models change by definition. The model_report() subtitle now calls it the deviance R², where it said pseudo-R².

  • For mixed models fitted by REML with lme4::lmer(), model_fit_table() now takes AIC, BIC and the log-likelihood from a maximum-likelihood refit and says so in a message. REML criteria cannot be compared between models with different fixed effects, which is the comparison the model-estimates vignette makes. If a refit fails, a warning says so and that model’s criteria are NA. The R2 column stays NA for mixed models, as the help page now documents.

  • A glm fitted with na.action = na.exclude broke the classification and diagnostic plots. Its fitted values are padded with NA to the length of the data while its response is not, and the plots paired the two. The ROC, precision-recall, threshold, gain and lift plots and the confusion matrix failed, and calibration_plot() silently dropped bins and drew the rest with other rows’ outcomes. In the Q-Q panel of residual_diagnostics_plot(), the quantile residuals set each response against another row’s fitted value, and for a Gaussian model they were all NA, so the panel was empty. All of them now use the model’s own unpadded components. residual_diagnostics_plot() and influence_plot() also leave the excluded rows out of their frames, for an lm as for a glm. They no longer warn about removing those rows, and the 2p/n leverage line of influence_plot() no longer counts them.

  • The quantile residuals in the Q-Q panel of residual_diagnostics_plot() ignored prior weights in Gaussian and Gamma models. Every observation was given the same scale, so a correctly specified weighted model showed spurious departures from the line. The weights now scale each observation’s variance, as they do in the fit.

  • A brms posterior passed as a posterior draws object was read as a plain table. frequentist_bayesian_plot() silently pooled b_Intercept with Intercept, the intercept brms reports for centred predictors, into one slab. It also drew the sampler’s log density and every random effect as parameters. posterior_plot() stopped with an error about duplicated factor levels. Draws objects now keep their population-level (b_) parameters, named without the prefix as for a brms fit, with a message naming what was dropped. A labels key for one of them is written without the prefix too. In both functions, two parameters whose draws would share a label are now an error, and lp__ and lprior are never drawn as parameters, whatever form the draws take. For a stanreg fit, the group-level b[...] and Sigma[...] draws are no longer read as fixed effects either.

  • When bayesian holds draws, frequentist_bayesian_plot() now draws only the terms both inputs share, and a message names any it dropped. A sigma in the posterior, or a frequentist term with no posterior, no longer takes a row of its own. Inputs that share no terms are an error.

  • A brms::fixef() matrix was read as draws, so it came out as four ‘parameters’ named after its columns. frequentist_bayesian_plot() now takes the summary path for it, and posterior_plot(), which needs draws, refuses it. The summary path also no longer warns about label keys you never supplied.

  • conf_level in frequentist_bayesian_plot() set the level of the frequentist intervals only. With draws, the half-eyes stayed at 66% and 95%, so conf_level = 0.8 drew 80% confidence intervals beside 95% credible ones, and nothing on the figure named either level. The level now sets the outer posterior interval too. The interval drawn when ggdist is not installed follows it, and so does the span that decides which faceted panels draw the reference line. The 66% inner interval is kept while conf_level exceeds 0.66, so that it stays the narrower of the two. A caption now names the level of each source’s intervals on either path, and the new caption argument replaces it or, with NA, omits it. A table of estimates keeps the intervals it holds, and the caption says that they are as supplied.

  • The two paths of frequentist_bayesian_plot() no longer swap the sources’ colours. With draws, the Bayesian half-eyes were brand blue and the frequentist overlay orange, the reverse of the forest plot drawn from summaries and of the Python package. The frequentist estimates are now brand blue and the Bayesian ones orange on both paths.

  • survival_plot() read the status coding separately in each group. Under the survival::Surv() 1/2 convention, a group whose subjects were all censored (all 1) fits the 0/1 convention as well, so it was read as a group in which every subject had the event, and its curve fell to zero. Codings that mixed the two conventions across groups were accepted silently. The coding is now read once, over all observations.

  • survival_plot() silently misread a factor status. The factor was coerced to its level codes and read under the 1/2 convention, so whichever level sorted first was taken as censored, whatever it meant. A character status became NA throughout, with only a coercion warning, and drew a flat curve at one. Both are now refused with an error that says to recode the indicator first.

  • survival_plot() ignored its group and status arguments when time was a data frame. It read both from conventionally named columns only (group, strata or arm, and status or event), so survival_plot(df, group = "treatment") drew a single pooled curve with no legend, log-rank test or risk-table rows. A column name or a vector with one entry per row is now honoured for both, and takes precedence over the conventionally named column. A name that matches no column is an error.

  • The number-at-risk table of survival_plot() could miscount at its default breaks. pretty() returns multiples of a binary floating-point step, so with follow-up up to 1.2 the break labelled 0.6 was 0.6000000000000001, and a subject followed up to exactly 0.6 was left out of the count there. A last break equal to the longest follow-up was lost the same way. The breaks are now rounded to their step before the counts are taken.

  • The median-survival guides of survival_plot() mislabelled some medians. The survival estimate was compared with 0.5 without a tolerance, so a step that the arithmetic left a rounding error above 0.5 was taken to stay above it. With times c(2, 3, 4, 8, 8, 10, 10, 11) and status c(1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1), the guide read ‘median 10’ where survival::quantile.survfit() gives 9. A curve that ended at 0.5 drew no guide. For a survfit object, the midpoint of a curve that sat at 0.5 was taken with the next row, which can be a censoring time at which the curve does not move. The medians now follow the rule of quantile.survfit(), including its tolerance and its midpoint for a curve that ends at 0.5, whatever the input and whether or not survival is installed.

  • save_plot() wrote files that fail the checks journals run on submitted figures. An EPS left out every translucent element, including all the points and the confidence band of the first scatter_trend() example, with only a terse device warning to show for it, and it named its fonts without embedding them. A PDF did not embed its fonts either. A TIFF was uncompressed: 8.1 MiB at the default 7 by 4.5 inches, and more than the 10 MB PLOS allows at the largest figure size it accepts. A transparent background, such as theme_void() leaves, could also give the TIFF the alpha channel PLOS refuses. PDF and EPS files now go through the cairo devices, which embed the fonts. An EPS rasterises its translucent layers, and whatever they overlap, at 600 dpi or more, with a message when it does. A TIFF is now LZW-compressed and drawn on white unless bg is given. On a Mac without ragg, it is drawn by the cairo TIFF device, because the default quartz one ignores compression. A device or device argument passed to save_plot() still wins. Without cairo, the old devices are used, with a message or a warning saying what the file lacks. R for macOS from CRAN loads cairo only where XQuartz is installed, so on a Mac without it a PDF or EPS is written this way, and a TIFF is left uncompressed unless ragg is installed.

  • effects_plot(), interaction_plot() and model_report() failed on any model with a transformed term (log(), poly(), ns(), scale(), factor(), I()) or an offset. Where a transformed term sat beside its raw variable, they drew a flat effect line or coincident interaction lines without complaint. The prediction grid is now built from the raw variables, so predict() re-applies every transformation, and offsets are held at their sample mean on the link scale, as the y-axis label now says. A model-frame name such as "log(rainfall)" stands for the variable it transforms, and the x-axis shows that variable.

  • The raw values behind a transformed term come from the data named in the model’s call. A model fitted to workspace vectors without data = is therefore refused, where it could silently plot its fitted values against the grid, and so is a data frame that has changed since the fit or a formula that reads one with $. A term computed from statistics of its rows, such as I(x - mean(x)), is refused as well, since predict() would compute it afresh over the grid. Beside its raw variable, such a term used to shift the line without complaint.

  • model_report() judged every glm by normal-theory panels. A correctly specified logistic model, simulated with 400 observations, put about a third of its standardised deviance residuals outside the Q-Q band, the picture of a broken model. A glm now gets the binned-residual and quantile-residual panels that residual_diagnostics_plot() already used, and model_report() gains the same glm_panels and seed arguments. glm_panels = FALSE restores the old panels. The help page of qq_plot() now says that the standardised deviance residuals of a non-Gaussian glm are not expected to be normal.

  • ts_forecast(), and the forecast overlay of timeseries_plot(), drew prediction intervals far too narrow. In rolling-origin backtests on eight classic series, the nominal 95% band covered about 60% of one-step-ahead outcomes. The documentation credited its square-root widening to seasonal naive forecasting, whose variance does not grow that way. Forecasts now come from a random walk with drift on the STL-seasonally-adjusted series, with the last seasonal cycle added back, which reproduces forecast::stlf(method = "rwdrift", s.window = "periodic"). A new lambda argument in both functions applies a Box-Cox (or log) transformation for a seasonal swing that grows with the level, and a caption on the overlay names the interval and the method. A series of exactly two cycles now gets the package’s own message, and decompose_plot() gains s_window. The vignette’s claim that STL lets the seasonal component evolve held only for a window this release exposes for the first time.

  • timeseries_plot() drew the forecast of a numeric x in the wrong place. The forecaster counted time in cycles from 1, while the history sits at the observation index or at the supplied time. The overlay therefore jumped back towards the start of the axis, and on a Date axis it landed in the year 4. The forecast now continues the history’s own axis, one typical step at a time. An unsorted time is also put in order before forecasting, as it already was for the moving average.

  • pca_plot() now fixes the aspect ratio, so the angles drawn between the loading arrows are their angles in loading space whatever the size of the device. The panel’s height and width follow the ranges of its axes, so a figure of another shape gains blank space around the panel. The arrows and their labels are drawn in a neutral dark grey (grey20) in place of the accent, which is also the palette’s fourth colour and so tied the variables to the fourth group. A misspelt group column, a column name passed with a prcomp object and a group vector of the wrong length are now errors. The first put one point in a level named after the misspelling and the rest in NA. The second put every point in one level named after the column, and the third was padded with NA or recycled in silence. group also takes an unquoted column name, as elsewhere in the package. A prcomp object fitted with retx = FALSE has no scores to draw, and it is now refused with a message that says so.

  • silhouette_plot() recoded the cluster labels it was given to 1, 2, 3 and so on, so a clustering labelled "low", "mid" and "high", or coded 2, 5 and 9, came back with other names in the band labels and in the attached "silhouette" table. The labels passed in are now kept, and the table’s neighbor column is a factor of them.

  • random_effects_plot() failed for any model with more than one random-effect term per grouping factor fitted without a correlation, (1 + x || g) for instance. The same error, “incorrect number of dimensions”, stopped split terms such as (1 | g) + (0 + x | g) and their glmer() equivalents. It now reads lme4’s conditional standard deviations for every model shape. For a correlated model, they equal the square roots of the diagonal it used before, so those intervals are unchanged. lme4 is now suggested at version 1.1-19 or later. Conditional variances for several terms per factor arrived in lme4 1.1-18, and 1.1-19 revised the data-frame method that reads them.

  • power_curve_plot() reads power tables with several curves, one per effect or design, and draws one line each, told apart by colour and line type. It joined them into a single zig-zag before. An effect, param or term column with more than one level separates the curves, with a message naming the columns used, and rows that share a sample size with no such column are now an error. It recognises n_subject and <power>_lo/<power>_hi columns such as pilotr’s, so the output of pilotr’s power_curve_mixed() plots as it is, with its band. It gains n, power, group, lower, upper and y_lab, appended after the existing arguments so that positional calls keep working. The y-axis title is “Power” for the usual power columns and the column’s name otherwise, so a decision probability such as pilotr’s p_meaningful is not labelled as power.

  • The grouped plots each treated a grouping variable in their own way. A numeric code, such as a block numbered 1 and 2, failed in scatter_trend() with “Continuous value supplied to a discrete scale”, and explore_distribution() and ecdf_plot() drew it as one ungrouped curve. A level with no rows, as subset() leaves in a factor, took a colour in the correlation panel of explore_pairs() but not in its scatter panels, so the levels after it changed colour from one panel to the next. group_comparison_plot() and raincloud_plot() warned that such a level had too few observations and kept an empty place for it on the axis, which group_comparison_plot() moved to the end. Missing groups made raincloud_plot() fail, were drawn as a grey group of their own by scatter_trend(), outlier_plot() and explore_pairs(), and vanished without a word elsewhere. scatter_trend(), explore_distribution(), ecdf_plot(), raincloud_plot(), group_comparison_plot(), explore_categorical(), explore_pairs(), ridgeline_plot() and outlier_plot() now share one rule. The group becomes a factor, so a numeric code is a group, but a numeric column with more than 20 distinct values is refused as continuous, as explore_categorical() already refused such an x. Rows with a missing group are dropped with a message, as survival_plot() drops them, and levels left without rows take no colour, legend key or place on an axis. Colours are matched to the levels by name, so a level keeps its colour in every layer and panel, and a group too sparse for a ridge no longer shifts the colours of the ridges after it. An unnamed palette is assigned to the levels in use in their order, and a named one still pins a colour to each level. explore_categorical() now orders its groups by level, where it sorted them alphabetically, so they take the same colours as in the Python package. explore_pairs() leaves a numeric group out of its default columns and stops with a clear error when cols names it. With the default palette, the warning that more than eight groups lose the colour-vision guarantee now comes once, when the plot is made, where it came each time the plot was drawn.

  • palette_preview(), confusion_matrix_plot() and correlation_heatmap() drew some labels below the 4.5:1 contrast that WCAG asks of text. The first two switched from white to dark grey text at a relative luminance of 0.4, although the two colours tie near 0.2. Four of the eight default swatches therefore had white labels at 2.85 to 3.87:1, and counts on mid-blue cells of a confusion matrix fell as low as 2.3:1. correlation_heatmap() drew white labels whenever |r| exceeded 0.6, which left the r = -0.70 of wellbeing_survey at 3.6:1, and its n/a sat in grey40 on a grey85 cell at 4.1:1. Each label is now black or white, whichever has the higher contrast against its tile as drawn, which is at least 4.58:1 on any colour. The tile colours are read as the fill scale draws them, interpolated in the Lab colour space, where the confusion matrix used an RGB approximation.

  • vif_plot() computed the VIFs of a weighted lm or a glm from the correlations of the design matrix, which leave out the weights of the fit. The generalised VIF of Fox and Monette (1992) compares the confidence region of a term’s coefficients with the one they would have without collinearity, so it depends on those weights. The VIFs now come from the covariance of the coefficients, as car::vif() computes them, and agree with it. For glm(adverse_event ~ biomarker + age + arm, family = binomial) fitted to clinical_trial, the VIF of age moves from 1.0073 to 1.0046. An unweighted lm with an intercept gives the values it gave before. A model fitted without an intercept now gives VIFs computed from columns that are not centred, with a warning, as car::vif() does.

  • A multivariate ts, such as cbind(mdeaths, fdeaths), or a numeric matrix was read as one series, its columns laid end to end. timeseries_plot() drew a single line. For a ts it zigzagged between the columns at every time, and for a matrix it ran on from one column into the next. acf_plot() returned the autocorrelation of the joined columns. seasonal_plot() and the classical decompose_plot() recycled the seasons and times of one column over all of them, so the columns were drawn over one another, and ts_forecast() forecast the joined columns at missing times. timeseries_plot() now draws one line per column, named after the columns. acf_plot(), decompose_plot(), seasonal_plot() and ts_forecast() refuse more than one column with a message that gives the count. They read a ts with a single column as that series. ts() makes one from a one-column data frame, and the STL decomposition stopped on it with “only univariate series are allowed”.

  • decompose_plot() and ts_forecast() now trim missing values at either end of a series, as the Python package does, so a forecast, the overlay of timeseries_plot() included, starts after the last observation. ts_forecast() and the STL decomposition stopped with the error “missing values in object” from stl(). A missing value inside the series is refused with a message that names x and asks for the value to be dropped or imputed, where stl() and decompose() stopped with errors of their own. acf_plot() still computes the correlations across such a gap from the pairs of observations present, with a warning, while the Python package refuses the series. The help pages of both packages now say so.

  • timeseries_plot() keeps the level order of a factor group, which sets the legend and the colours, and leaves out levels that no row uses. It ordered the groups by first appearance.

  • timeseries_plot() drew a moving average over an even window, such as rolling = 12 for monthly data, half an observation early. Equal weights over twelve observations are centred between two of them, and the mean of observations 1 to 12 was drawn at observation 6, where its centre is 6.5. An even window now gives the 2×12 moving average (Hyndman & Athanasopoulos, 2021, Section 3.3), a 12-point average followed by a 2-point one, which is centred on each observation and is the trend that decompose() estimates. The caption of a grouped overlay names it, and the window needs a series one observation longer than itself. The Python package drew the same average half an observation late, and the two packages now draw the same values. An odd window is unchanged.

Degenerate input

  • survival_plot() truncated a non-integer status code, so c(0, 0.5, 1) was read as two censored observations and an event. Non-integer codes are now refused with the existing coding message.

  • survival_plot() kept an arm whose every status was missing when group was a factor. The arm stayed in the legend with no curve and a row of zeros in the risk table, and logrank = TRUE failed with an error that did not say why. The arm is now dropped with the missing statuses, as it already was for a character group.

  • vif_plot() refuses a model with aliased coefficients, for which no VIF exists, and names the terms they belong to. It failed with an unrelated base-R error, “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”.

  • seasonal_plot() refused every frequency that is not a whole number, such as the 365.25 / 7 of weekly data, with a message about season_labels that no labels could satisfy, while decompose_plot() drew the same series. Such a frequency is now rounded down to whole seasons, counted from the first observation as stl() counts them, and a message says so.

Auditing a finished figure

  • check_figure() measured all text against the plot background, so text on a coloured facet strip or legend box was judged against a background it is not drawn on: white strip text on a dark strip failed and unreadable grey strip text passed. Each text is now measured against its own background, with a translucent fill taken as the colour it shows over what lies beneath it. Large text (18 pt, or 14 pt bold, as printed) is held to the 3:1 that WCAG asks of it, where it used to be held to 4.5:1. The text_contrast row reports the text that falls furthest short of its own threshold and gives that threshold, and its detail names the text’s printed size and weight. A translucent plot or panel background is also measured as the colour it shows. Its alpha used to be dropped, so geometry_contrast moves for such a figure. The relative-luminance code now cites the current WCAG 2.2 definition and its 0.04045 breakpoint, which changes no ratio.
  • check_figure() measured translucent marks and text as if they were opaque, so a figure could pass contrast, colour-vision and greyscale checks that its drawn colours fail. The ‘mended’ example in the Get started vignette was one: its points, drawn at alpha 0.7, passed the geometry check at 3.87:1, and the vermillion a reader sees reaches 2.56:1. Colours are now composited over their background with the alpha each geom applies, outlines drawn opaque are credited, and the colours of each aesthetic are compared among themselves. A translucent colour or text is named in the detail with its alpha and the colour it is drawn as, and the separability rows say whether their closest pair are colours or fill colours. Verdicts on translucent figures can change in either direction. The vignette’s example now draws its points opaque.
  • check_figure() now treats a colour or fill mapped in several layers, one value per layer, as the encoding it is. Such figures were reported as encoding nothing by colour. With red and green drawn one group per layer, every colour row read “not applicable”, whereas the same figure drawn in one layer fails the deuteranopia check at 0.37. frequentist_bayesian_plot() with draws, whose half-eyes and frequentist overlay are separate layers, was never audited for colour. It now is, and the orange of its half-eyes fails geometry_contrast at 2.25:1, as that colour does on white in any figure. Shape and line type split across layers count towards redundant_encoding in the same way. A colour set as a constant, as in geom_point(colour = "red"), is still left out, as the help page now says.
  • check_figure() gains an annotation_text_size row for the text drawn inside the panel: annotations, the labels of layers such as geom_text() and geom_label(), and the cell values and labels of depictr’s own plots. The text-size check never saw that text, so a 5.7 pt annotation passed a 6 pt floor while the report gave 8.80 pt as the smallest text. The new row holds it to the same floor at its printed size. It is appended last, so the report now has ten rows. The contrast of that text is not measured, and nor is text a layer builds only when it is drawn, such as ggrepel’s labels. When all of a figure’s text is inside the panel, the two rows for the text around it no longer say that the figure draws no text.
  • The colour rows of a figure coloured by a continuous scale, such as a heatmap, said that nothing was distinguished by colour. They now say that colour is a continuous scale, which these checks do not audit, and the documentation recommends a perceptually ordered map such as viridis for one. The help page and the README now also give the default palette’s contrast limit, which the Get started vignette already stated: four of its eight colours fall below the 3:1 that WCAG asks of a graphical object against white, the orange from the second group on. The documentation shows how to audit a figure saved at its final width, with that width given as both widths or neither, and the help page gives four publishers’ text floors, dated and linked, where it called 6 pt a common publisher floor.
  • check_figure() accepts a multi-panel composite and audits each panel on its own, in the order patchwork tags them, with a leading panel column. It used to refuse one, which left the package’s own composites without an audit. Among them are the figures of arrange_plots(), residual_diagnostics_plot(), model_report(), estimation_plot() and survival_plot(risk_table = TRUE). Each panel’s legend is measured with the panel. A spacer or a guide area takes no panel number, and a wrapped element, such as a grob or a table, is left out with a warning. Composite-level titles and tags are not measured.
  • check_figure(max_text_pt =) checks a ceiling as well as a floor, and save_plot(check = TRUE) audits the figure at the width it is saved at, so the text sizes are the printed ones. The ceiling adds a last row, text_size_max, for the largest text at its printed size, around the panel and inside it, and that row passes at or below its threshold. Nature, for one, allowed no text above 7 pt but the panel labels. Without max_text_pt, the report keeps its ten rows. save_plot(check = TRUE) gives the saved width, converted to centimetres from inches, millimetres or pixels, as both width_cm and render_width_cm. It warns with each check the figure fails and attaches the report to the file name it returns, as attr(, "check").

Metadata and documentation

  • The declared ggplot2 floor rises from 3.5.0 to 3.5.2. The current patchwork cannot load against ggplot2 3.5.0 or 3.5.1, so every function that composes panels failed on the floor the package declared: arrange_plots(), model_report(), residual_diagnostics_plot(), estimation_plot(), explore_pairs(), decompose_plot() and survival_plot(risk_table = TRUE). On ggplot2 3.5.x, pca_plot() and silhouette_plot() also warned about an unknown linewidth and drew borders round their labels. They now name the border argument each ggplot2 version understands and draw no border on either. The reference lines of coefficient_plot(), frequentist_bayesian_plot() and posterior_plot() no longer warn about an unknown inherit.aes on ggplot2 3.5.x. The floors job in continuous integration now also tests the floor against the newest patchwork, and runs every example with warnings treated as errors.

  • ragg is listed in Suggests. save_plot() asks whether it is installed when it chooses a device for a TIFF, and R CMD check warns about a package looked up that way unless the package declares it.

  • citation("depictr"), the website and CITATION.cff give the DOI that CRAN assigned to the package, https://doi.org/10.32614/CRAN.package.depictr, in place of the Zenodo concept DOI. It names the R package across all its versions, and it is the DOI that the CRAN page and the citation R generates for a CRAN package already gave, so the package no longer circulates under two. Zenodo still archives every GitHub release, and CITATION.cff lists both identifiers. Its release date is now the day CRAN published 0.3.0, 2026-09-01, where it gave a date that matched neither CRAN nor the GitHub release. The CRAN DOI and the Zenodo DOI are shown as full links on the website and in the README, and the sidebar of the home page shows the CRAN DOI once: the DOI badge in the README no longer appears there a second time.

  • posterior_plot() and frequentist_bayesian_plot() formatted a label for every posterior draw, which made a ten-parameter figure take seconds and a full brms draws object minutes. Labels are formatted once per parameter. format_terms() now strips the b_ and bs_ prefixes from a whole vector with one regular expression. It split each term on its colons and took about 15 seconds for 40,000 labels, a job that now takes a fraction of a second. An unnamed labels vector, one label per parameter in the order of draws, now works in posterior_plot(). It failed with a message that counted the draws as terms. The two bootstrap tests that took most of the test time are skipped on CRAN and still run in continuous integration.

Changed defaults

  • The gap statistic’s default search in k_diagnostic() and cluster_plot(suggest_k = "gap") could not return k = 1, so it reported clusters in pure noise (k = 2 for 20 of 20 seeded Gaussian data sets). k_range now defaults to NULL, which searches 1:8 for the gap and elbow criteria and 2:8 for the silhouette, as before. A suggestion made with the old default can change, so pass k_range = 2:8 to reproduce it. The help pages now say that the elbow never chooses the first or last candidate.

  • standardise = TRUE in coefficient_plot(), and so the default model_report(), multiplied every model-matrix column by its standard deviation. That made a factor contrast depend on how the groups happened to be balanced: one true effect of 1 came out as 0.52, 0.43 or 0.23 with 50%, 20% or 5% of observations in the group. It also scaled an interaction by the spread of a product column, 265 for rainfall:treatment in the crop-yield model. Continuous inputs are now scaled by their standard deviation, and factor, logical and two-valued inputs such as 0/1 are left as they are (Gelman, 2008). An interaction is scaled through its continuous inputs, so rainfall:treatment becomes the change in the rainfall slope per SD of rainfall. The new sd_multiple = 2 gives Gelman’s two-SD convention. poly(), ns() and other matrix-valued terms are left unscaled with a message. An interaction of continuous inputs draws a warning unless they are all centred, because each main effect is a slope at zero on the other input. The axis label adds “(contrasts unscaled)” when a contrast is drawn, and the model_report() panel is titled “Coefficients (per SD of continuous predictors)”. The help page and the model-estimates vignette no longer claim that the standardised magnitudes are comparable.

  • binned_residual_plot() draws its band from the model, as twice the standard error of a bin’s mean residual that the fitted model implies. The old band, twice the standard deviation of the bin’s residuals over the square root of its count, collapsed wherever a bin held no events. On the package’s own example, a correctly specified model, it flagged five of seventeen bins. When the adverse events were redrawn 200 times from the fitted model, so that each refit was correct by construction, the old band flagged 31% of the bins and the new one 3%. The binned-residual panel that residual_diagnostics_plot() and model_report() draw for a glm changes with it. band = "empirical" reproduces the earlier figure, whose band is the one arm::binnedplot() draws. Observations with zero prior weight, which take no part in the fit, are now left out of the bins.

  • survival_plot() draws log-log confidence limits by default. They stay between 0 and 1 and cover better in small samples than the untransformed Greenwood limits it drew before (Borgan & Liestøl, 1990). The new conf_type argument restores those with "plain" and gives the default of survival::survfit() with "log". The limits of a survfit object were copied from the object, at the level and on the scale it was made with, so conf_level was ignored and a 90% band showed the object’s 95% limits. They are now recomputed from the object’s standard errors at the requested conf_level and conf_type, so they equal those that survfit() gives with the same conf.int and conf.type. An object made with conf.type = "none" keeps its standard errors, so it now gets limits as well, which conf_level = NA leaves out. An object without standard errors, or one whose lower limits follow conf.lower = "peto" or "modified", keeps its own limits, with a warning when they differ from those requested. Where a curve falls to zero, the limits keep the values of the step before, so a band drawn from follow-up times no longer stops one event early. A conf_level outside (0, 1), such as 95 meant as a percentage, is now an error.

  • The cycle lines of seasonal_plot(style = "season") start from a colour that clears 3:1 against white. They took the sequential ramp of depictr_palette(), which starts at #e6eff5, 1.16:1 against white, so the earliest cycles were close to invisible. With twelve cycles, four of the lines fell below the 3:1 that WCAG 2.2 asks of a graphical object. The ramp now runs from #4a8fc0, at 3.51:1, through the brand blue to #08315a, and palette still replaces it. The sequential palette keeps its pale end for fills. Past about six cycles, neighbouring lines take colours too close to tell apart, as the help page now says, and style = "subseries" keeps each cycle in its own place on the axis.

  • Colour separability in palette_safety() and check_figure() is now measured with CIEDE2000 (Sharma, Wu & Dalal, 2005). The 1976 Euclidean distance it replaces overstates differences between saturated colours: ggplot2’s default five-colour palette was certified safe under deuteranopia, though two of its colours become almost identical, 2.74 apart in CIEDE2000. The threshold stays at 5, and the Okabe-Ito palette’s closest pair now measures 6.43, where it measured 7.4. depictr_palette(9) already warned that interpolated colours lose the guarantee, and its nine colours now fail the check too. metric = "cie76" restores the old measure for this release, and the greyscale check is the lightness gap under either.

  • simulate_cvd() at partial severity now uses Machado et al.’s published matrices, interpolated between the tabulated severities. Interpolating towards normal vision missed them on the default palette by up to 11 units of the 1976 Delta-E, or 6.2 in CIEDE2000. Full-severity results, and so palette_safety(), palette_preview() and check_figure(), are unchanged. The authors tabulate a matrix for each tenth of severity, and a severity between two tenths now takes the linear interpolation of the two, as the colorspace package does, whose output it matches. The old transform drew the full-severity matrix towards the identity. Between severities 0.3 and 0.7, it moved the palette’s colours too little under protan and deutan and too far under tritan, so under a red-green deficiency they looked further apart than the model predicts.

  • Confidence intervals for a glm whose dispersion is estimated (the Gaussian, Gamma, inverse Gaussian and quasi families) now use the t distribution on the residual degrees of freedom, matching the t tests of summary.glm() and the lm path. They used z and were about 10% too narrow at 12 residual degrees of freedom, so a Gaussian glm disagreed with lm() on the same model. At 100 degrees of freedom, the two differ by about 1%. The choice is read from the model’s own summary, so binomial, Poisson and MASS::glm.nb() fits keep z, as do mixed models. tidy_estimates(), coefficient_plot(), compare_models(), frequentist_bayesian_plot() and model_report() change with it, and so do the bands of effects_plot() and interaction_plot(). In the Python twin the intervals follow the fitted result’s use_t, which gives the same t intervals.

  • The coefficient of a two-level factor is now labelled with its level, treatment: enhanced, as the coefficients of factors with more levels already were, so the row says which contrast it shows. It was labelled treatment, which hid the direction of the contrast. Interaction rows name their levels the same way, rainfall × treatment: enhanced where they showed rainfall × treatmentenhanced. The labels change in coefficient_plot(), compare_models(), frequentist_bayesian_plot() and optimizer_fixef_plot(). compare_models() now takes them from every fitted model it is given, so a factor term that only a later model holds is labelled too. A named labels vector still sets any label, and labels = c(treatmentenhanced = "treatment") restores the old one. The Python twin now labels its terms by the same rules.

New features

  • depictr_palette(order = "contrast"), also accepted by scale_colour_depictr() and scale_fill_depictr(), reorders the built-in palette so that up to three groups pass every colour check of check_figure(), contrast against white included, and up to four keep 3:1. It leads with the brand blue, the vermillion and the reddish purple, then the bluish green. It warns past four colours. The ramps refuse it, and a palette set with depictr_options(palette = ) is returned as it was set, with a warning. depictr_options(palette = depictr_palette(order = "contrast")) makes the order the default for every later plot. The default order is unchanged, and the Python twin gives the same order.

  • simulate_figure() shows a finished figure, legend and colourbar included, as a reader with a colour-vision deficiency sees it. It builds the grob table of a ggplot or a patchwork and passes every colour in it through simulate_cvd(). That covers the line and fill colours of each grob and the cells of each raster, and each colour keeps its alpha. It returns a gtable, which grid::grid.draw() draws and save_plot() saves. Recolouring the data before the plot is built would have left the legend keys and colourbars in their original colours. The Python twin’s simulate_figure() uses the same matrices on the pixels of the rendered figure.

  • exponentiate = TRUE in tidy_estimates(), coefficient_plot() and compare_models() gives odds, rate or risk ratios, and the two plots draw them on a log axis with the reference line at 1. The axis is labelled “Odds ratio” for a logit link, “Rate ratio” for a log link in a Poisson, quasi-Poisson or negative binomial model, “Risk ratio” for a binomial model with a log link and “exp(Estimate)” otherwise. tidy_estimates() exponentiates the estimates and interval limits and leaves std.error on the link scale, as broom::tidy() does. Its glm method used to swallow the argument and return log-odds. coefficient_plot() exponentiates after standardise, so a standardised slope becomes a ratio per SD of its predictor. A data frame of estimates is read on the link scale. reference_line now defaults to 1 when exponentiating and to 0 otherwise. The Python twin gains the same arguments.

depictr 0.3.0

CRAN release: 2026-09-01

Auditing a finished figure

  • New check_figure(), an accessibility and honesty audit of the figure you are about to submit. Until now the package could vouch for its palette and say nothing about a finished plot, which is the thing a reader sees. Give it anything a depictr function returns, including a plot extended afterwards with +, and it introspects the build and returns a tidy table. The rows cover the separability of the encoding colours under each dichromacy and in greyscale, the smallest text size against a stated physical output width, the WCAG contrast of the text and of the geometry against their backgrounds, and whether any distinction is carried by colour alone. Every row carries the value it measured beside the threshold it was measured against, so a verdict can be argued with.
  • The colour-vision helpers are exported. simulate_cvd() and palette_safety() were internal here while the Python twin exported both, so the advertised parity did not hold. They now match in name, arguments, return shape and refusal wording. simulate_cvd() gains a severity argument and returns lower-case hex, as the Python twin does. palette_safety() returns the full report, naming the worst condition, the closest pair and the verdict. The old return was a bare vector of distances.
  • The accessibility claim has been narrowed to what is true. The default eight-colour palette clears every colour-vision check and fails the new greyscale check: its orange (#e69f00) and sky blue (#56b4e9) differ by 0.79 in CIE lightness, so a black-and-white printer renders them as the same grey. The Okabe-Ito guarantee is about hue confusion and was never a claim about greyscale. The threshold stays where it is, and vignette("depictr") now states the limitation where the claim is made, so the package’s own defaults are held to the same standard as anybody else’s.

Figures that misreported the data

  • quantile_residuals() produced nonsense for a cbind(successes, failures) binomial model. The two-column response matrix was flattened to a vector and the raw success counts were then multiplied by the trial totals a second time, so the residuals of a well-specified model centred far from zero and the Q-Q diagnostic looked catastrophically misspecified. The matrix response now supplies its counts and trial totals directly, and the residuals are standard normal again where they should be.
  • ridgeline_plot() stacked its overlaps upside down. The row sort meant to draw the top ridge first is a no-op, because ggplot2 draws ribbon groups in factor-level order, so each upper ridge painted over the one below it, the opposite of the conventional ridgeline overlap. The draw order is now carried by the group aesthetic, with the colour assignment unchanged.
  • random_effects_plot(sort = TRUE) froze every facet in the first facet’s order. With more than one term the level factor was shared across panels, so only the first panel came out sorted and the rest zig-zagged. Each facet now orders its own levels, with the plain level names kept on the axis.
  • A user-supplied title in power_curve_plot() is no longer run through format_terms(), which turned a colon into a multiplication sign and blanked underscores. Only a title recovered from the power-curve object, which is a raw term name, is tidied.
  • survival_plot() drew a phantom arm for a group that does not exist. An NA in group became a level of its own, matching no observation, so the plot gained an all-censored curve for a group nobody was in, and under logrank = TRUE it failed outright. Missing groups are now dropped with a message saying how many.
  • survival_plot() silently discarded non-finite follow-up times. Dropping a case from a Kaplan-Meier fit changes the denominator, and so every step of the curve and every cell of the number-at-risk table, while the figure carries no trace of it. It now refuses them, with the same message as the Python twin, since whether to drop or impute is the analyst’s decision to make. This replaces a silent drop, so it is a behaviour change for anyone who relied on the old handling.
  • depictr_palette() interpolated past its accessibility guarantee without saying so. Beyond the eight Okabe-Ito base colours the palette is a ramp, and the colour-vision-deficiency guarantee that is this package’s reason for existing stops holding, so the interpolated palette fails the package’s own safety check. It now warns at the point of interpolation, and only for the built-in palette, since a user-supplied one carries no such claim. The documentation is qualified to match.
  • summary_table() counted missing-group records in Overall and in no group column, so the per-group sizes silently fell short of the headline N. They now get a Missing column of their own.
  • A seeded plot leaked its seed into the caller’s random stream in a session that had not yet drawn a random number, so the documented reproducibility guarantee quietly failed in exactly the fresh session that would rely on it.
  • compare_models(facet = TRUE) now honours depictr_options(reference = ) for its per-panel reference line. seasonal_plot() no longer labels a frequency-7 series Mon..Sun, an alignment a plain ts cannot know. And a mistyped labels key now warns, so the raw parameter name no longer sits on the plot.

Degenerate input

  • survival_plot() now says when it drops observations with a missing status, in the wording of the missing-group message. The drop was previously silent. A status that is missing for every observation is an error. This brings the third kind of incomplete survival input into line with the other two, a missing group being announced and a non-finite time refused.
  • silhouette_plot() checks that clusters has one entry per row of data before dropping incomplete rows. A vector sized to the complete rows used to slip past the late check, because subsetting it with the logical index padded it with NA, and then died in the distance computation. It is now refused with the same message cluster_plot() uses.
  • tidy_estimates() no longer fails on a rank-deficient lm with a raw “differing number of rows” error. confint() keeps aliased terms as NA rows while coef(summary()) drops them, so the intervals are now cut to the estimated terms, with a message naming the aliased terms that were left out.
  • cluster_plot() and k_diagnostic() drop zero-variance columns with a message when scale = TRUE, as correlation_heatmap() already did, so a raw k-means error no longer escapes. k_diagnostic() now names the values of k_range it cannot evaluate instead of dropping them from the search without a word, and explore_pairs() labels an undefined correlation n/a where it once printed r = NA beside a raw stats::cor() warning.

Metadata and documentation

  • The declared minimum dependency versions are now installed and tested by a CI job. The patchwork floor is raised from 1.2.0 to 1.3.0. That was verified by running it: 1.2.0 cannot run model_report() at all, because patchwork::free(type =, side =) arrived in 1.3.0.
  • gain_plot() documents that the perfect-model reference line is drawn for a single model only, which is what the code has always done, and a test now pins it. The line bends at the prevalence of the outcome, and overlaid models need not share a prevalence.
  • model_fit_table() documents that a single model is enough, which is what the code always accepted, and raincloud_plot() no longer claims to be built from base graphics primitives: like ridgeline_plot(), it is base R and ggplot2 alone.
  • ?depictr again lists every exported function (scale_fill_depictr() and the scale_color_depictr() alias were missing), the README no longer describes the Python package as a feature-parity twin (its own README says otherwise), CONTRIBUTING no longer claims the maintenance workflows close their own issues, and the standardise = TRUE axis label now names the x-only convention the figure uses.
  • The README no longer opens with a link to the documentation site, which on the site’s own home page pointed the reader at the page in front of them.
  • Every vignette now turns console colour off and fixes the console width while it renders. pkgdown passes the calling terminal’s colour support into its build subprocess, so a coloured message or error would otherwise reach the reader as escape sequences in the middle of the text.

depictr 0.2.2

Examples that match the chart

  • The precision-recall, gain and lift examples move to an outcome with a scarce positive class, which is the case those charts are documented for. They previously ran on an outcome that was 94 per cent positive, so the gain curve sat on the diagonal and lift hovered at one.
  • The calibration example fits a model and plots its predicted probabilities, since a reliability curve is a check on a fitted model.
  • The power-curve article names the effect the shipped simulation actually covers, and its no-simr branch reads a summary derived from that simulation, so the two branches agree by construction.

Fixes

  • vif_plot() restricts its scale to the severity levels present, which removes an empty key entry from the rendered figure.

depictr 0.2.1

Documentation

  • The introductory vignette shows depictr_palette() returning the palette’s hex colours directly, ready for scale_fill_manual() or a base-graphics col = argument, and shows depictr_options() setting defaults for every later plot and returning the previous values, so the earlier look can be put back afterwards.
  • vignette("diagnostics-and-uncertainty") saves an arranged panel with save_plot(), which writes at a print-ready 300 dpi by default and creates any missing directories.
  • vignette("multivariate-and-survival") adds k_diagnostic(method = "gap"), which compares within-cluster dispersion against a null reference and so, unlike the other two criteria, can support k = 1.
  • vignette("time-series") adds classical decomposition, which holds the seasonal component fixed across the series where STL lets it evolve from year to year.
  • The optimizer_fixef_plot() and power_curve_plot() reference pages describe what each plot shows. Both pages previously described the prototype gists the plots grew from.
  • On the documentation site, source chunks are set a little smaller than the output and the prose, so a typical line fits the narrower home and article columns without horizontal scrolling, and the copy button stays attached to its code block.

depictr 0.2.0

Fixes

  • roc_curve_plot() rejects a ci that resolves to fewer than one bootstrap resample, with a clear error. Until then it drew an all-NA band and an [NA, NA] AUC annotation, saying nothing.

Data

  • In wellbeing_survey, region now shifts stress and income, which flow through to life satisfaction. The region-grouped plots (faceted densities, ridgelines, the region dendrogram) therefore compare four distinct distributions where earlier they compared four samples of one. The bundled datasets are regenerated by data-raw/generate_datasets.R as before.

Citation

  • The package citation (inst/CITATION and CITATION.cff) carries the Zenodo concept DOI, and the citation title uses sentence case.

Documentation

  • The package overview (?depictr) lists every exported function and all five bundled datasets. Previously several functions and two datasets were missing.
  • The vif_plot() example fits deliberately collinear predictors, so the plot shows inflated VIFs sitting above the threshold line. The earlier example produced near-identical bars around 1, with the line off the axis.
  • depictr_options() describes what brand and accent actually drive, and depictr_palette() notes that qualitative colours interpolated beyond the base set are not guaranteed to stay distinguishable under colour-vision deficiency.
  • lift_plot() documents its own top-right inside-legend corner rather than inheriting gain_plot()‘s bottom-right wording, and DESCRIPTION notes that composite panels return ’patchwork’ objects.
  • References throughout the documentation follow APA 7 and carry DOIs, and spelling is consistently British (en-GB).
  • The documentation site’s home page is restructured around a pitch, gallery and signposts. The time-series decomposition example draws its trend confidence band. LICENSE.md carries the full MIT text so the site’s licence page renders in full, as in the sibling packages.

Packaging and checks

  • Example variants that render several multi-panel figures (posterior_plot(), residual_diagnostics_plot(), decompose_plot()) are wrapped in \donttest{} so each example file stays within CRAN’s five-second budget. The first call of every example still runs.
  • CITATION.cff and the test artefact Rplots.pdf are excluded from the build tarball, and the test that produced Rplots.pdf draws to a null device instead.
  • New tests pin the legend_inside gates. The legend moves inside the panel when a plot’s gate is satisfied, and the theme is left alone when it is not.

depictr 0.1.1

  • Documentation and packaging polish, with no change to the plotting API.
  • The documentation site adopts the shared house style used across the package family, with a citation page carrying a copyable and downloadable BibTeX entry.
  • Consolidated to a single LICENSE file, and added community and contribution files.

depictr 0.1.0

First release. depictr is a unified, consistent toolkit of publication-ready plots spanning the whole analysis workflow. It grew out of, and generalises, three earlier plotting functions (frequentist_bayesian_plot, plot.fixef.allFit and powercurvePlot).

Exploring data

  • explore_distribution(), explore_categorical(), explore_bivariate(), explore_pairs(), correlation_heatmap(), missingness_map(), outlier_plot(), raincloud_plot(), group_comparison_plot(), scatter_trend() and summary_table().
  • estimation_plot() for estimation statistics: group effect sizes (mean differences, Cohen’s d / Hedges’ g) with bootstrap confidence intervals, in the spirit of the ‘new statistics’.
  • ecdf_plot() (empirical cumulative distribution, optionally by group), ridgeline_plot() (overlapping per-group densities) and dumbbell_plot() (a connected two-group comparison across categories).
  • explore_distribution() gains facet to draw one panel per group instead of overlaying them (much clearer beyond a few groups), and correlation_heatmap() gains reorder to cluster correlated variables together.

Multivariate, clustering and survival

  • pca_plot() and scree_plot() (principal component analysis), cluster_plot() (k-means on principal-component axes) and dendrogram_plot() (hierarchical clustering), and survival_plot() (Kaplan-Meier curves with a number-at-risk table, median survival and an optional log-rank test, all computed in base R).
  • silhouette_plot() and k_diagnostic() help choose and validate the number of clusters (silhouette widths, plus elbow and average-silhouette diagnostics).

Time series

  • timeseries_plot() (one or more series with an optional moving average), acf_plot() (autocorrelation / partial autocorrelation) and decompose_plot() (trend / seasonal / remainder decomposition).
  • seasonal_plot() (seasonal subseries) and ts_forecast() (a simple, dependency-free forecast with prediction intervals).

Model estimates and inference

  • tidy_estimates() provides the shared tidy estimate table, with methods for lm, glm, merMod and data frames and a fallback to broom::tidy().
  • coefficient_plot(), compare_models(), frequentist_bayesian_plot(), effects_plot(), interaction_plot(), random_effects_plot(), optimizer_fixef_plot() and model_fit_table().
  • frequentist_bayesian_plot() now draws the full Bayesian posterior for each term as a half-eye density and overlays the matching frequentist point estimate and confidence interval, so the two inferential frameworks can be compared directly. It reads posterior draws from brmsfit, stanreg, draws/matrix objects or a data frame.

Diagnostics and classification

  • residual_diagnostics_plot(), influence_plot(), qq_plot(), vif_plot(), roc_curve_plot(), pr_curve_plot(), gain_plot(), lift_plot(), calibration_plot() and confusion_matrix_plot().
  • binned_residual_plot() (binned residuals for logistic and other GLMs, with approximate error bounds) and threshold_plot() (classification metrics across decision thresholds, highlighting Youden’s J and the maximum-F1 cut-off).

Uncertainty and power

  • posterior_plot() summarises posterior draws with a choice of styles ("halfeye", "interval", "gradient" or "dots") and can annotate a region of practical equivalence (ROPE) and the probability of direction.
  • power_curve_plot() for power-analysis curves (e.g. from simr).

Theming and reporting

  • theme_depictr(), depictr_palette(), scale_colour_depictr() (and scale_color_depictr(), scale_fill_depictr()), palette_preview(), format_terms(), model_report() (a one-figure model overview), arrange_plots() and save_plot().
  • depictr_options() sets package-wide defaults once, covering the brand and accent colours, qualitative palette, base font size and family, and the colour used for missing values. Every plot and scale then honours them.

Layout and legibility

  • coefficient_plot(), compare_models(), posterior_plot() and frequentist_bayesian_plot() gain a facet/scales option that lays each term out in its own free-scaled panel, so terms on very different scales (a large intercept alongside small slopes) stay legible instead of being squished onto the zero line. frequentist_bayesian_plot() uses this layout by default.
  • Every plot has had a pass for legibility. silhouette_plot() cluster labels no longer clip. raincloud_plot() uses one colour per group across all layers. dendrogram_plot() hides leaf labels for large trees. confusion_matrix_plot() picks each label’s colour from the tile luminance. gain_plot() and lift_plot() label their reference lines. timeseries_plot() shows a single legend, and k_diagnostic() now returns the diagnostic curve as a plot.
  • coefficient_plot() gains standardise, scaling each coefficient by its predictor’s standard deviation so magnitudes are comparable. model_report() uses it by default, removing the empty band in its coefficient panel.
  • vif_plot() shows the ordinary VIF (not its square root) for single-df terms, scales the axis to the data, and draws a single clearly-labelled threshold line (reported in the caption when it is off-axis), leaving no wide empty band or hard-to-read guides.
  • seasonal_plot(style = "season") reverses its sequential legend so the darkest, most-recent cycle sits at the top, matching the plotted order.
  • Factor coefficient names are prettified by default to the effect (variable) name in coefficient_plot(), compare_models() and frequentist_bayesian_plot(), where they are read from the model, so conditionunrelated becomes condition and word_frequency becomes word frequency. optimizer_fixef_plot() and posterior_plot() gain a labels argument for the same. Any user-supplied labels take precedence. pca_plot() likewise shows underscores in its loading-arrow labels as spaces (soil_ph -> soil ph).
  • Redundant cluster legends are dropped: silhouette_plot() (the bands are labelled in place) and cluster_plot() when the centroids are labelled.
  • survival_plot() has been tidied in several ways. The log-rank annotation renders a proper chi-squared and an italic p, formatted APA style (no leading zero, p < .001 below that threshold). The median guide is labelled median <value>. The y-axis title margin is tighter, and the colour legend and the number-at-risk table list the groups in the same order, following the group factor’s levels.
  • A legend_inside argument (off by default) draws the legend inside the panel, over a semi-transparent background, in a corner the plot usually leaves empty, which reclaims the right-hand margin. It is offered by roc_curve_plot(), gain_plot(), lift_plot() (bottom-right / top-right of the curve), ecdf_plot(), survival_plot(), explore_distribution(), dumbbell_plot() and missingness_map(). For any other plot the same is one theme() call, and vignette("exploring-data") shows how, alongside tidying legend titles.
  • theme_depictr() now centres legend titles over their keys, which reads more tidily than ggplot2’s default left alignment, especially for an inside or a top/bottom legend.
  • estimation_plot() reserves more headroom above the lower panel so the effect-size annotation (Hedges’ g / Cohen’s d) is never clipped.
  • scree_plot() colour-matches and names its dual axes, ‘Variance explained (bars)’ on the left and ‘Cumulative (line)’ on the right.
  • Statistical letters are italic in annotations: the log-rank p, model_report()’s n and R, and estimation_plot()’s g / d.
  • British (en-GB) spelling throughout: the crop_yield column is now fertiliser, coefficient_plot()/model_report() take standardise, and confusion_matrix_plot() takes normalise.

Data

  • Five reproducibly simulated datasets: lexical_decision (counterbalanced priming experiment), wellbeing_survey (with realistic missingness), crop_yield (a fertiliser-by-treatment field trial), clinical_trial (right-censored survival with a rare adverse event) and monthly_sales (two seasonal retail series).

Accessibility

  • The qualitative palette is based on the colourblind-safe Okabe-Ito set (led by the depictr brand blue), and depictr_palette() provides sequential and diverging variants. palette_preview() can show any one, or all three, and can simulate deuteranopia, protanopia or tritanopia so a palette’s legibility can be checked directly.

Notes

  • Heavier modelling back-ends (lme4, broom, simr, survival, brms, posterior, ggdist, cluster, boot) are in Suggests and used only when available, so the package installs and checks without them. Vignettes draw on small precomputed model fits shipped in inst/extdata/, so they knit without a Bayesian or mixed-model toolchain.
  • Functions with an optional seed (cluster_plot(), qq_plot() and residual_diagnostics_plot()) restore the caller’s random number generator state afterward, so passing one for reproducibility has no side effect on your own subsequent random draws.
